_: german-sounds.json — the table behind decks/German-Sounds-and-Spelling.folio-deck.json, read by build-german-sounds.js. NOTHING IN IT IS COMPOSED. Every `like` (the English sound a letter resembles) is the 'English approximation' cell of Wikipedia's Help:IPA/Standard German at the revision in `sources.ipa`, with its own regional labels (DE, AT, CH; RP; Scottish). Every `when` and every `ipa` of a consonant row is a cell of the Consonants table of 'Grapheme-to-phoneme correspondences' in Wikipedia's 'German orthography' at the revision in `sources.orthography`; a vowel row's `ipa` is the symbol of the Help:IPA row its `like` comes from. Every `says` is a sentence, or a marked cut of one, of 'German orthography' (the sections Umlaut diacritic usage, Capitalization, Vowel length and Short vowels) — except the two stress rows, which are sentences of Wikipedia's 'Standard German phonology' at the revision in `sources.phonology` (section Stress). Wiki markup is turned into <b>, <i> and ⟨ ⟩, a link becomes its text, a footnote is dropped, a cut inside a passage is marked […], and nothing is reworded. The transcription beside an example word in `words` is the first pronunciation the English Wiktionary gives that word (kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16), copied, and it is there so that a word chosen by hand can be checked: `words` is used wherever the spelling alone does not decide the sound (a long or a short ä, ö, ü; s before a vowel; v; a final b, d or g; where the stress falls). `rx` is NOT from the articles: it is how the builder finds, among the one-word headwords of the Goethe A1 deck (the article taken off, lower case), the first three words in the order the deck is dealt that show a row whose sound the spelling decides; `mark` is which letters of a `words` row are picked out. A row no A1 headword shows is not carded. The letters that sound as an English speaker expects (f, k, l, m, n, p, t and, before a vowel, b, d, g) have no card.

vowels.says: Mostly, the long vowel /iː/ is represented in writing by the digraph ⟨ie⟩, for instance in Liebe ('love'), hier ('here').

rules.name: the umlaut
rules.says: The accented letters ⟨ä, ö, ü⟩ are used to indicate the presence of umlauts (fronting of back vowels). […] When it is not possible to use the umlauts (for example, when using a restricted character set) the characters ⟨Ä, Ö, Ü, ä, ö, ü⟩ should be transcribed as ⟨Ae, Oe, Ue, ae, oe, ue⟩ respectively […]; simply using the base vowel (e.g., ⟨u⟩ instead of ⟨ü⟩) would be wrong and misleading.

rules.name: a long or a short vowel
rules.says: A doubled consonant after a vowel indicates that the vowel is short, while a single consonant often indicates the vowel is long, e.g. Kamm ('comb') has a short vowel /kam/, while kam ('came') has a long vowel /kaːm/. […] A silent ⟨h⟩ indicates the vowel length in certain cases.

rules.name: the capital letter
rules.says: A typical feature of German spelling is the general capitalization of nouns and of most nominalized words. In addition, capital letters are used: at the beginning of sentences […]; in the formal pronoun Sie 'you' and the determiner Ihr 'your' […].

rules.name: where the stress falls
rules.says: In German words there is always one syllable carrying main stress, with all other syllables either being unstressed or carrying a secondary stress. […] Traditionally, word stress is seen as falling onto the first stem syllable.

rules.name: a verb with a prefix
rules.says: Words beginning with be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp- and a few other inseparable prefixes are stressed on the root. Words beginning with the separable prefixes ab-, auf-, ein-, vor-, and most prepositional adverbs are stressed on the prefix.
